## What does 2S-PA estimate?

Researchers often use scale means or factor scores to study relations among
constructs such as depression, motivation, or cognitive ability. These scores
are useful summaries, but they contain measurement error. Treating them as
error-free variables in a regression or path analysis can bias the estimated
structural relations (Cole & Preacher, 2014).

Two-stage path analysis (2S-PA; Lai & Hsiao, 2022) separates the analysis into
two stages. In **stage 1**, researchers fit measurement models and obtain
factor scores and estimates of their measurement error. In **stage 2**, the
factor scores serve as indicators of latent variables in a structural model.
Their loadings and error variances are fixed using the stage-1 results.
The structural coefficients therefore describe relations among the latent
variables, rather than relations among scores treated as perfectly reliable.

Joint SEM estimates the measurement and structural parameters simultaneously.
With 2S-PA, researchers can evaluate the measurement models separately and
retain the same measurement results when considering different structural
models. This is one of several approaches to *stepwise estimation* of latent
variable models reviewed by Vermunt (2025).

The simulation studies in Lai and Hsiao (2022) and Lai et al. (2023) found
results similar to joint SEM in large samples, with better convergence and
inference in some small-sample conditions. Those findings depend on the
models and conditions studied; they do not imply identical estimates in
every application.

## Example: industrialization and political democracy

We use `PoliticalDemocracy`, also used in the
[lavaan SEM tutorial](https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/sem.html).
The constructs are industrialization in 1960 (`ind60`) and political
democracy in 1960 and 1965 (`dem60` and `dem65`).

```{r load-pkg, message=FALSE}
library(lavaan)
library(R2spa)
```

### Stage 1: obtain scores for each construct

The measurement syntax is the same as in lavaan. Here, `local = TRUE`
fits a separate single-factor CFA for each construct. Each score uses
only the indicators of its own construct.

```{r}
measurement_model <- '
  ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
  dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8
'
fs_dat <- get_fs(PoliticalDemocracy, model = measurement_model, local = TRUE)
head(fs_dat[c("fs_ind60", "fs_dem60", "fs_dem65",
              "fs_ind60_se", "fs_dem60_se", "fs_dem65_se")])
```

The `fs_` columns contain the factor scores. The corresponding `_se`
columns contain their **standard errors of measurement**: uncertainty in
the scores due to imperfect measurement. These differ from the sampling
standard errors of the path coefficients that we obtain in stage 2.

Regression factor scores are used by default. They are shrinkage estimates,
so their loadings on the latent variables need not equal one. `get_fs()`
also stores these loadings and the score error variances for use in stage 2.

### Stage 2: estimate the structural relations

Write the structural model using the latent-variable names, without the
`fs_` prefix. `tspa()` adds the score indicators and their measurement-error
constraints automatically.

```{r}
path_model <- '
  dem60 ~ ind60
  dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60
'
tspa_fit <- tspa(model = path_model, data = fs_dat)
standardizedSolution(tspa_fit) |>
  subset(op == "~")
```

The `dem65 ~ dem60` coefficient describes the association of democracy in
1960 with democracy in 1965, holding industrialization constant. In the
standardized solution, a one-SD difference in the predictor corresponds
to an `est.std`-SD difference in the outcome. The SDs refer to the latent
variables after accounting for measurement error.

Unstandardized coefficients depend on how the latent variables are scaled.
They can be substantively useful when that scale has a meaningful interpretation.
Standardized coefficients are particularly useful when comparing 2S-PA with
joint SEM or across scoring methods, because the latent-variable metrics
may differ (Lai et al., 2023).

The returned object is a lavaan fit. Use `summary(tspa_fit, standardized = TRUE)`
for the full output. To see the score loadings and error variances fixed in
the stage-2 model, inspect the generated lavaan syntax:

```{r}
cat(attr(tspa_fit, "tspaModel"))
```

## Using an existing CFA fit

If you have already fitted and evaluated a measurement model in lavaan,
pass that fit to `get_fs()`. The following example fits the three factors
together, allowing their correlations to be estimated in stage 1.

```{r}
cfa_fit <- cfa(measurement_model, data = PoliticalDemocracy)
fs_joint <- get_fs(cfa_fit)
tspa_joint <- tspa(path_model, data = fs_joint)
standardizedSolution(tspa_joint) |>
  subset(op == "~")
```

With regression scoring from a multi-factor model, a score can use indicators
of other correlated factors. As a result, it can load on more than one latent
variable, and its measurement error can correlate with that of other scores.
`tspa()` retains both features using the information stored by `get_fs()`.
See [Multi-Factor Measurement Model](multiple-factors.html) for an explanation
and a comparison with separate measurement models.

## Mean scores

2S-PA can also account for measurement error in unweighted item means.
`method = "mean"` computes the mean of the indicators assigned to each factor
and obtains its loading and error variance from the measurement model.

```{r}
fs_mean <- get_fs(PoliticalDemocracy,
                  model = measurement_model, method = "mean")
tspa_mean <- tspa(path_model, data = fs_mean)
standardizedSolution(tspa_mean) |>
  subset(op == "~")
```

This option requires complete indicator data. The mean-score loading is
generally not one, even when every item loads on only one factor.

## Multiple groups

The `HolzingerSwineford1939` data contain cognitive test scores from two
schools. We illustrate a model relating visual ability to speed. First,
fit a multigroup CFA with equal factor loadings across schools:

```{r}
hs_model <- '
  visual =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  speed =~ x7 + x8 + x9
'
hs_fit <- cfa(hs_model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939,
              group = "school", group.equal = "loadings")
fs_hs <- get_fs(hs_fit)
tspa_hs <- tspa("visual ~ speed", data = fs_hs, group = "school")
standardizedSolution(tspa_hs) |>
  subset(op == "~")
```

The stage-2 path is estimated separately for each school, using each group's
score loadings and error variances. To constrain the unstandardized paths
to equality, add `group.equal = "regressions"` to `tspa()`.

Measurement invariance should be evaluated in stage 1. If only partial
invariance is supported, specify the appropriate equality constraints and
freed measurement parameters in that model before obtaining scores.
The stage-2 correction then uses the group-specific measurement information
(Lai et al., 2023). A common latent-variable metric is needed for meaningful
cross-group comparisons.

`standardizedSolution()` uses within-group SDs, so even equal unstandardized
paths can have different standardized values. For coefficients expressed in
grand-SD units across the combined sample, see
[Grand Standardized Coefficients](gr-std-coef.html).

## How the score measurement information is represented

For a vector of factor scores, the stage-2 measurement equation is

$$
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_i = \mathbf{b}_i +
\mathbf{L}_i\boldsymbol{\eta}_i + \mathbf{e}_i,
\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{e}_i) = \mathbf{T}_i.
$$

Here, $\boldsymbol{\eta}_i$ contains the latent variables, $\mathbf{L}_i$
contains the score loadings, $\mathbf{b}_i$ contains the score intercepts,
and $\mathbf{T}_i$ contains the score error variances and covariances.
`get_fs()` stores these quantities as data-frame attributes named `fsL`,
`fsb`, and `fsT`. They are used automatically by `tspa()`.

| Example column or attribute | Interpretation |
| --- | --- |
| `fs_ind60` | Factor score for industrialization |
| `fs_ind60_se` | Standard error of measurement of that score |
| `ev_fs_ind60` | Score error variance |
| `ind60_by_fs_ind60` | Loading of `fs_ind60` on `ind60` |
| `ecov_fs_ind60_fs_dem60` | Measurement-error covariance between two scores |
| `attr(fs_dat, "fsL")` | Score loading matrix; rows are scores, columns are latent variables |
| `attr(fs_dat, "fsT")` | Score error variance-covariance matrix |
| `attr(fs_dat, "fsb")` | Score measurement intercepts |

If you supply scores from another source, you can specify `fsL` and `fsT`
explicitly. The simpler `se_fs` argument specifies standard errors of
measurement for single indicators with unit loadings and uncorrelated
measurement errors. That parameterization must match the scale of the scores;
it should not be assumed for shrinkage scores.

For complete continuous-item CFA data, these quantities are constant within
a group. With missing indicators, categorical items, or random effects from
mixed models, they can vary across observations. `tspa()` pools varying
quantities within groups; `tspa_mx_model()` retains the observation-specific
values using OpenMx *definition variables*. A definition variable is a data
value used to fix a model parameter for a particular observation.

Keep the row order of a `get_fs()` result when passing it to another function:
its row-specific attributes must remain aligned with the scores. To analyze
a subset, obtain scores for that subset. For separately scored constructs,
`combine_fs()` preserves the measurement information and can align observations
by an ID column; see the multi-factor vignette.

  *Psychological Methods, 27*(4), 568–588. <https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000410>
- Lai, M. H. C., Tse, W. W.-Y., Zhang, G., Li, Y., & Hsiao, Y.-Y. (2023).
